content_html_sanitized:
Posted July 2, 2002
(MarijuanaNews note: While Americans, Canadians, and citizens of other countries with well-developed economies and democratic institutions naturally focus on the harm done by cannabis prohibition to their own citizens, we too often overlook the damage being done in poor countries.

The story below is not the sort that I would usually post, but it presented an opportunity to make a point: that cannabis prohibition is even worse in many countries that can afford it even less than DEAland.

The Philippines, as a former DEAland colony, is probably more susceptible to DEAland prohibitionist propaganda than others, but it is hardly unique. Thailand, which ironically means " land of the free, " is also in the midst of a media-fed " anti-drugs " hysteria. Of course, it is not just DEAland prohibitionist propaganda, but strong political and economic pressure that pushes these policies.

Now, let it be said that DEAland is by no means responsible for all of the evil being done by prohibition in developing countries. In most developing countries, prohibition presents an irresistible temptation to increase police powers and thus the opportunity for more bribes, in cultures where police corruption is already endemic. Some countries would have cannabis prohibition, even if DEAland and the other western democracies did not. And, as in the wretched story below, their own media are every bit as craven and incompetent as those in DEAland.

However, all of them naturally look to DEAland and other technologically advanced countries for the pseudoscientific justification for prohibition. Indeed, an official from a developing country might find it inconceivable that " the leader of the free world " -- noted for its science would promote bad public policies with bad science.

The good news is that some countries, notably Mexico and Jamaica, are recognizing cannabis prohibition for what it is, a counterproductive DEAland fraud, and they are looking for a way out.

This is very fortunate for DEAland's real national interests, as opposed to the ideological fixations of the appalling people who govern us.

The political and economic stability of Mexico should be our highest strategic objective, but it is being subordinated to the drug war.

And then there is the urgent need for medical access to cannabis in developing countries that are too poor to be able to afford pharmaceuticals, even if they worked.

For better or worse, the idea of a separate category for " medical " cannabis is simply impossible in these countries. There are not enough doctors, or anything else in their " health care systems " so only fully legalizing cannabis would make medical access possible.

In any case, the week in which both Canada and DEAland celebrate their " freedom " seems like a good time to note that others deserve real freedom, too. )

June 29, 2002
From The Philippine Star

DEATH FOR MARIJUANA

A Malabon City judge yesterday meted the death penalty to a big-time drug pusher and a life term to his cohort after they were caught with some 25 kilos of marijuana bricks in a buy-bust operation by police anti-narcotics operatives in March this year.

Eduardo Limpin, 24, single, jobless, of 42 University Avenue, Potrero, Malabon, who is to die by legal injection, was also given life imprisonment for illegal possession of a kilo of dried marijuana leaves.

His co-accused, Ricky America, 32, single, jobless, also of the same place, was sentenced to life imprisonment for illegal possession of some two kilos of dried marijuana bricks.

In a 15-page decision, Judge Benjamin Aquino ( Branch 72 ) also directed Limpin to pay a fine of P15 million for the two cases. America was ordered to pay a fine of P5 million for his case.

Court records showed that Limpin and America were apprehended by elements of the Northern Police District-Drug Enforcement Unit during a buy-bust operation last March 15 in front of their house.

Police managed to close a deal with the accused after a police informant tipped them off of the duo's illegal activities. Limpin was arrested while handing over a kilo of dried marijuana worth P1,500 to a police poseur-buyer.

After a search was made at Limpin's house, some 22 kilos of marijuana wrapped in newspaper in a styropor box were found by the police team while two kilos of the prohibited drug were also seized from America.

The two denied the charges in open court with the alibi that they were framed up by the police and that the dried marijuana, believed to have come from Mt. Province, was planted on them.
(MarijuanaNews note: Two points. First, Canadian prohibitionists please take note, the cannabis was domestic, so even the threat of the death penalty does not deter growing.
See

Second, I obviously have no idea whether the police planted the evidence in this case, it even happens in the most advanced countries. This is the most dangerous form of police corruption.)

Aquino junked the defense after finding sufficient evidence against the two to convict them.
